slides.title: Filiform and fungiform papillae
slides.desc: Two kinds of papilla side by side: pointed, keratinised filiform on the left, a blunt rounded fungiform on the right.
slides.caption: Filiform papillae are hard and pointed, lack taste buds, and increase friction between the tongue and food. Fungiform papillae are blunt elevations scattered among them on the margin and tip of the tongue, and they do carry taste buds.

slides.title: Tongue, dorsal surface
slides.desc: The rough upper surface, thrown into closely packed filiform papillae over a thick epithelium.
slides.caption: Dorsal surface of the tongue. The specialised mucosa carries papillae; filiform papillae dominate and give the surface its velvety texture. Beneath the epithelium lie the lamina propria and then the interlacing skeletal muscle of the tongue.

slides.title: Tongue, ventral surface
slides.desc: A smooth, thin, non-keratinised lining with no papillae — the opposite of the dorsal surface.
slides.caption: Ventral surface of the tongue, covered by lining (non-keratinised stratified squamous) mucosa rather than the specialised mucosa of the dorsum. There are no papillae; the epithelium sits on a thin lamina propria, with skeletal muscle beneath.

slides.title: Tongue, full thickness
slides.desc: Papillae on the surface, lamina propria beneath them, and bundles of skeletal muscle cut in two planes at the base.
slides.caption: A full-thickness section of tongue. The muscle layer is the giveaway: skeletal muscle bundles run in three planes, so the same field shows some cut in cross section and others cut longitudinally. Seromucous (von Ebner) glands extend down into that muscle.

hotspots.label: Skeletal muscle cut in cross section

slides.title: Circumvallate papilla
slides.desc: A large dome of mucosa sunk into the surface, with a deep moat-like furrow around it.
slides.caption: Circumvallate papillae are 1 to 2 mm across and sit in a V just in front of the sulcus terminalis. The central elevation is surrounded by a furrow, or trench; taste buds line the wall of the furrow, and the ducts of the serous glands of von Ebner open into the bottom of it to rinse it clean.

hotspots.label: Taste buds in the furrow wall

slides.title: Taste bud
slides.desc: A pale barrel of cells spanning the epithelium, opening at the surface through a taste pore.
slides.caption: Taste buds contain gustatory (receptor) cells, supporting cells and basal precursor cells. A tastant dissolved in saliva reaches the microvilli of the receptor cells through the taste pore and triggers depolarisation. The five basic stimuli are sweet, bitter, sour, salty and umami.

hotspots.label: Stratified squamous epithelium of the furrow wall

slides.title: Serous acini and a duct
slides.desc: A duct cut in cross section, ringed by its own epithelium, with deeply stained serous acini all around it.
slides.caption: Serous cells have a round nucleus in the basal third and apical secretory (zymogen) granules, which is why they stain so strongly. An acinus is a blind sac of such cells draining into the duct system: intercalated duct, then striated duct, then excretory duct.

hotspots.label: Secretory granules in the apical cytoplasm

slides.title: Parotid gland, low power
slides.desc: A purely serous gland broken up by large empty-looking spaces — the adipose cells that are typical of the parotid.
slides.caption: The parotid is completely serous, has many striated ducts, and characteristically contains adipose tissue. The facial nerve courses through it. Saliva from here is watery and rich in amylase.

slides.title: Parotid gland, striated duct
slides.desc: A striated duct cut across the middle of the field, surrounded by uniformly serous acini.
slides.caption: Striated ducts concentrate the secretion by pumping water back into the connective tissue. The base of each cell is thrown into deep folds packed with mitochondria, and it is those folds that give the basal edge its striated look under the light microscope.

slides.title: Sublingual gland, low power
slides.desc: Pale, washed-out acini fill almost the whole field — the look of a gland that is mostly mucous.
slides.caption: The sublingual is the smallest of the three major glands and is mixed but predominantly mucous, with few ducts. Mucous cells look empty because the mucinogen dissolves out in routine preparation, leaving a pale cytoplasm and a flattened nucleus pressed against the base of the cell.

slides.title: Sublingual gland, high power
slides.desc: Pale mucous acini with flattened basal nuclei, capped here and there by a darker crescent of serous cells.
slides.caption: A mixed acinus is a mucous acinus with a cap of serous cells — the serous demilune. The demilune is now known to be partly an artefact of traditional fixation, but it is still how a mixed acinus is recognised in these sections.

hotspots.label: Mucous cells with flattened basal nuclei

slides.title: Submandibular gland, low power
slides.desc: Mostly dark serous acini with scattered pale mucous ones, and plenty of striated ducts.
slides.caption: The submandibular gland is mixed but mostly serous, and striated ducts are conspicuous. Saliva contains amylase, lysozyme and secretory IgA.

slides.title: Submandibular gland, high power
slides.desc: Serous acini with round basal nuclei and granular cytoplasm, next to pale mucous acini capped by demilunes.
slides.caption: At this magnification the difference between the two secretory cells is clear: the serous cell has a round nucleus and apical zymogen granules, the mucous cell a flattened basal nucleus and a pale, washed-out cytoplasm. Where both occur in one acinus the serous cells form a demilune.

slides.title: Oesophagus, wall
slides.desc: A folded lining of thick stratified squamous epithelium over a submucosa that contains its own mucous glands.
slides.caption: The mucosa is thrown into longitudinal folds that are flattened as a bolus passes. Submucosal glands are tubuloacinar, arranged in small lobules and drained by a single duct; they are one of the features that identifies oesophagus. The muscularis has an inner circular and an outer longitudinal layer.

slides.title: Oesophagus, muscularis and myenteric plexus
slides.desc: Two muscle layers running at right angles to each other, with a nerve plexus sandwiched between them.
slides.caption: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus always lies between the inner circular and the outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa, and it controls the strength and rhythm of contraction. In the upper third of the oesophagus both layers are skeletal muscle, in the middle third they are mixed, and in the lower third both are smooth muscle.

hotspots.label: Outer longitudinal layer, cut in cross section

slides.title: Oesophagogastric junction
slides.desc: An abrupt change along the surface, from a thick many-layered lining on one side to a single layer of tall cells with pits on the other.
slides.caption: The transition from the stratified squamous epithelium of the oesophagus to the simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium of the cardiac stomach is abrupt, not gradual. The change is called the epithelial transformation zone, and the gastric side can be recognised at once by its pits and coiled cardiac glands.

slides.title: Stomach wall and a ruga
slides.desc: A large fold of the whole mucosa and submucosa standing up into the lumen, with the muscle layers beneath.
slides.caption: Rugae are temporary folds of mucosa plus submucosa that flatten out as the stomach fills; they are not permanent like the plicae circulares of the small intestine. This section shows the full thickness of the wall: mucosa, submucosa and muscularis externa.

slides.title: Gastric mucosa, low power
slides.desc: A surface pitted with narrow invaginations, glands packed beneath them, and a thin band of muscle closing off the base.
slides.caption: The gastric mucosa has three parts: the surface epithelium that dips down as gastric pits, the glands that open into the bottom of those pits, and the muscularis mucosae. There are no villi — that is what separates stomach from small intestine at a glance.

slides.title: Gastric pits and glands
slides.desc: Deep surface pits above, glands running down to a muscular band below.
slides.caption: Several gastric glands empty into the base of each pit. The cells lining the pit are surface mucous cells, which secrete a thick alkaline mucus loaded with bicarbonate and protect the lining from both abrasion and acid.

slides.title: Gastric gland, full depth
slides.desc: A single gland followed from the surface pit down to the muscularis mucosae, changing character as it goes.
slides.caption: A fundic gland has three levels. The pit and isthmus are lined by surface mucous cells; the neck holds mucous neck cells and most of the parietal cells; the base is crowded with chief cells. Parietal cells sit in the upper two thirds, chief cells at the bottom.

hotspots.label: Parietal cells in the upper two thirds

slides.title: Gastric gland, special stain
slides.desc: A stain that picks out the mucus at the surface in dark purple and leaves the large pale cells of the gland below it.
slides.caption: The darkly stained mucus marks the surface mucous cells and the pits. Below them the plump, pale, triangular cells with a central round nucleus are parietal cells; they produce hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. The cells at the very base of the gland are chief cells.

hotspots.label: Chief cells at the base of the gland

slides.title: Chief and parietal cells
slides.desc: Two cell types side by side: smaller cells crowded with magenta granules, and larger pale triangular ones.
slides.caption: Chief cells are typical protein-secreting cells, with abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, basophilic basal cytoplasm and apical zymogen granules of pepsinogen. Parietal cells are larger, pyramidal, with eosinophilic cytoplasm, an intracellular canalicular system lined by microvilli, abundant mitochondria and a tubulovesicular system.

legend.v: Apical granules of pepsinogen in chief cells
Pepsinogen-secreting cell at the gland base
HCl and intrinsic factor secreting cell

slides.title: Cardiac region of the stomach
slides.desc: Shallow pits over short glands that are cut at every angle, because they coil at their lower end.
slides.caption: Cardiac glands are simple tubular and coiled at the lower end, which is why one section shows them cut across, obliquely and lengthwise all at once. They are lined by mucus-secreting cells and resemble the cardiac glands of the oesophagus.

hotspots.label: Cardiac glands cut at different angles

slides.title: Fundic and cardiac glands meeting
slides.desc: Two kinds of gland in one field: long straight ones on one side, short coiled pale ones on the other.
slides.caption: The border between the fundic and the cardiac regions. Fundic glands are long and straight and contain parietal and chief cells; cardiac glands are shorter, coiled and purely mucous. The pits are relatively shallow in both.

slides.title: Fundic versus cardiac glands
slides.desc: A dashed line down the middle separates glands packed with pink cells from paler, emptier ones.
slides.caption: On one side the fundic glands contain parietal cells, so the gland looks solid and eosinophilic. On the other the cardiac glands are mucous, so they look pale and the lumen is easy to see. A lymphatic nodule sits in the lamina propria at the base.

hotspots.label: Lymphatic nodule in the lamina propria

slides.title: Gastric glands, high power
slides.desc: Large pale triangular cells bulging from the wall of some glands, and clear open lumina in others.
slides.caption: At high power the parietal cell is unmistakable: large, pyramidal, with a round central nucleus and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, bulging out from the side of the gland. The paler glands on the right are cardiac and purely mucous, with a wide lumen.

slides.title: Enteroendocrine cells, immunostain
slides.desc: Scattered brown-stained cells sitting at the base of otherwise blue-grey glands.
slides.caption: Enteroendocrine cells, also called argentaffin cells or the diffuse neuroendocrine system, are stained here with a brownish reaction product. Their secretory granules lie toward the basal membrane, because the hormones are released into the blood rather than into the lumen.

slides.title: Enteroendocrine cell, electron micrograph
slides.desc: A single cell at very high magnification, with dense granules collected along its base near a vessel.
slides.caption: The granules of an enteroendocrine cell are concentrated at the basal pole, next to the basal lamina and the capillary, which is how a hormone-secreting cell is arranged. Products include gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin, GIP, motilin and ghrelin.

hotspots.label: Secretory granules at the basal pole
Basal pole against the blood vessel

slides.title: Pyloric region of the stomach
slides.desc: Very deep pits taking up much of the mucosa, with short branched pale glands crowded beneath them.
slides.caption: Pyloric glands are simple tubular and branched at the very lower end. The pits are deeper here than anywhere else in the stomach, so in a section the pit occupies about half the thickness of the mucosa. The glands are lined by mucus-secreting cells whose nuclei are flattened against the base of the cell.

hotspots.label: Deep pit (foveola) lined by mucus-secreting cells

slides.title: Pylorus
slides.desc: A mucosa of deep pits and pale glands on one side of the field, with a thick band of muscle filling the other.
slides.caption: The pylorus is the tapering end of the stomach. Its glands are mucous, its pits deep, and the inner circular layer of the muscularis externa is greatly thickened here to form the pyloric sphincter. The lettering on this plate is the lecturer’s own self-test.

slides.title: Small intestine, scanning electron micrograph
slides.desc: A ring of wall seen in three dimensions, its inner surface completely covered with finger-like projections.
slides.caption: Villi are folds of mucosa projecting into the lumen that greatly increase the absorptive surface. The surface is amplified at four levels: plicae circulares (mucosa plus submucosa), villi (mucosa only), crypts, and finally the microvilli of the enterocyte itself.

hotspots.label: Submucosa and muscularis of the wall

slides.title: Duodenum
slides.desc: Broad leaf-shaped villi above, and in the submucosa beneath the muscle band, a layer of pale glands.
slides.caption: The duodenum is identified by its submucosal Brunner glands, which no other part of the gut has. They secrete an alkaline, bicarbonate-rich mucus that neutralises the acid chyme arriving from the stomach, and their ducts drain into the crypts of Lieberkuhn. Its villi are leaflike rather than finger-like.

slides.title: Jejunum
slides.desc: Tall, slender, finger-like villi standing close together, with nothing in the submucosa below.
slides.caption: The jejunum has the longest, most finger-like villi and the best developed plicae circulares, and it has neither Brunner glands in the submucosa nor Peyer patches. It is identified by what it lacks as much as by what it has.

slides.title: Ileum
slides.desc: Shorter villi, and a large pale mass of lymphoid tissue bulging up from beneath the mucosa.
slides.caption: The ileum is identified by its Peyer patches: large aggregates of lymphatic nodules that extend from the lamina propria down into the submucosa. Its villi are shorter than those of the jejunum, and M cells overlie the patches.

slides.title: Villi and crypts of the small intestine
slides.desc: Villi cut lengthwise with crypts opening between their bases, and pale glands below the thin muscle band.
slides.caption: Crypts of Lieberkuhn are invaginations of the surface epithelium at the base of the villi. Cells there are mostly in stages of development, migrating up toward the surface to replace enterocytes. The pale glands beneath the muscularis mucosae are Brunner glands, so this is duodenum.

hotspots.label: Lamina propria in the core of a villus

slides.title: Brush border and goblet cells, PAS stain
slides.desc: A sharp magenta line along the free surface of the epithelium, with darker flask-shaped cells scattered through it.
slides.caption: PAS stains carbohydrate, so it picks out two things at once: the glycocalyx coating the microvilli of the enterocytes, seen as a continuous striated border, and the mucin inside the goblet cells. The lettering on this plate is the lecturer’s own self-test.

hotspots.label: Lamina propria in the core of the villus

slides.title: Crypt of Lieberkuhn, electron micrograph
slides.desc: The lower half of a gland at very high magnification, its cells filled with large round granules.
slides.caption: Paneth cells sit at the base of the crypt and have the ultrastructure of a protein-secreting cell. They secrete lysozyme, an antibacterial enzyme, other antimicrobial compounds, and defensins that attract lymphocytes and dendritic cells. Mitotically dividing stem cells lie just above them.

legend.v: Granule-filled cells at the base of the crypt
Lymphatic capillary in the lamina propria

hotspots.label: Plasma cell in the lamina propria

slides.title: Peyer patches
slides.desc: A row of large pale lymphoid masses sitting side by side under the lining, pushing the surface up between the villi.
slides.caption: Peyer patches are aggregates of large lymphatic nodules in the ileum, extending through the lamina propria into the submucosa. M (microfold) cells overlie them: flattened cells with folds instead of microvilli that take up antigen from the lumen and hand it to the lymphocytes in their intracellular pockets.

hotspots.label: Lymphatic nodule of a Peyer patch
Lymphatic nodule of a Peyer patch

slides.title: Colon
slides.desc: A flat surface with no projections at all, and straight test-tube glands running down from it packed with pale cells.
slides.caption: The colon has a smooth surface with no villi. Its tubular glands, or crypts of Lieberkuhn, run perpendicular to the surface, are deeper than those of the small intestine and contain a far higher proportion of goblet cells. Absorptive and mucus-secreting cells reabsorb electrolytes and water.

slides.title: Large intestine, scanning electron micrograph
slides.desc: A ring of wall in three dimensions whose inner surface is smooth, without any finger-like projections.
slides.caption: The layers of the large intestine are the same as those of the small intestine, but the surface carries no villi. The main job of this mucosa is absorbing water, sodium, vitamins and minerals, which concentrates the chyme into semisolid faeces.

hotspots.label: Mucosa, smooth and free of villi
Submucosa and muscularis of the wall

slides.title: Appendix, wall
slides.desc: A narrow lumen with a few tubular glands, surrounded by sheets of densely packed small dark cells.
slides.caption: The appendix is a blind evagination off the caecum and a significant part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue. Lymphocytes infiltrate the lamina propria and lymphatic follicles fill the mucosa and submucosa. Mucosal folds project into the lumen, but villi are absent and the tubular glands are lined by abundant goblet cells.

hotspots.label: Tubular glands lined by goblet cells

slides.title: Rectum
slides.desc: Straight, closely packed glands filling a smooth-surfaced mucosa, with a large open vessel in the tissue below.
slides.caption: The rectum keeps the pattern of the colon: no villi, and long straight tubular glands rich in goblet cells. The distended blood vessel in the submucosa is worth noting, since the venous plexus here is what becomes varicose in haemorrhoids.

slides.title: Recto-anal junction
slides.desc: Glands stop abruptly at one point along the surface, and beyond it the lining thickens into many layers with no glands at all.
slides.caption: At the recto-anal junction the simple columnar epithelium with its glands gives way to stratified squamous epithelium. The two things to notice are the absence of glands and the absence of a muscularis mucosae beyond the transition. Compare it with the oesophagogastric junction, where the change runs the other way.

slides.title: Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus
slides.desc: A pale band running diagonally between two sheets of smooth muscle, holding a small cluster of large nerve cell bodies.
slides.caption: The myenteric plexus lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa, where it coordinates the strength and rhythm of peristalsis. The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is the other half of the enteric nervous system and lies in the submucosa. The lettering here is the lecturer’s own self-test, with the plexus at b.

hotspots.label: Smooth muscle cut in cross section
